records.source: Ὄφελον ἀνείχεσθέ μου μικρόν τι ἀφροσύνης· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀνέχεσθέ μου.
records.gloss: Would that you were bearing with me a little something of foolishness; but indeed bear with me.
pieces: I wish you would put up with a little foolishness from me. Yes, do bear with me.

L.1: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. But indeed, bear with me.

R.1: I hope you will put up with me while I act a little like a fool. Please be patient with me.

decisions.choice: foolishness: the senseless talk of a boaster
alternatives: the foolishness of the message of the cross (1 Corinthians 1-3)
decisions.reason: ἀφροσύνης begins the passage that runs to 12:11, in which Paul plays the part of a fool and boasts as his rivals do (11:16-18; 12:11). The word, with ἄφρων ("fool"), means lacking good sense. It is a different word from μωρία and μωρός in 1 Corinthians 1-3, where the cross looks foolish to the world but is God's wisdom. Here the foolishness is Paul's own pretended folly, put on so that he can answer the boasting of others.

decisions.choice: an appeal: do bear with me
alternatives: a statement: indeed you are bearing with me
decisions.reason: ἀνέχεσθέ can be an imperative ("bear with me") or an indicative ("you are bearing with me"). After the wish in the first half, an appeal fits well, and the verb comes back in verses 4, 19 and 20, where the Corinthians bear with the rivals all too easily. Read as a statement, Paul would be saying, with some irony, that they are already doing so.

decisions.choice: I wish: a wish Paul is not sure will be granted
decisions.reason: Ὄφελον introduces a wish (as in 1 Corinthians 4:8 and Galatians 5:12). Paul is not certain that the Corinthians will listen.

decisions.choice: act a little like a fool
decisions.reason: Readable says what the foolishness is: Paul is about to speak as a fool would (m1). "Fool" and "foolishness" are kept through 11:1-12:11 at every level, so the reader can follow Paul's fool's speech.

records.heading: Paul and the false apostles

records.source: ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς θεοῦ ζήλῳ, ἡρμοσάμην γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἑνὶ ἀνδρὶ παρθένον ἁγνὴν παραστῆσαι τῷ Χριστῷ·
records.gloss: I am jealous for you with God's jealousy, for I betrothed you to one husband, a virgin pure to present to the Christ;
pieces: My jealousy for you is the jealousy of God {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}. I have pledged you in marriage to one husband: I mean to bring you to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} as a pure virgin bride.

L.2: For I am jealous over you with a jealousy of God, for I betrothed you to one husband, a pure virgin to present to {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.2: I care about you with the same jealous love that God has for you. You are like a young woman promised in marriage to one man, and I am like the father who arranged it. I want to bring you to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} pure, as a bride who has kept herself for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} alone.

decisions.choice: God's own jealousy: a protective love that will not share the beloved
alternatives: a godly jealousy, meaning simply a good kind of jealousy
decisions.reason: θεοῦ ζήλῳ is "with a jealousy of God": the jealousy Paul feels is God's own for his people, not envy or suspicion. In the Old Testament God is jealous for his people as a husband for his wife (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Hosea 2:19-20). Paul shares that jealousy because someone is trying to win the Corinthians away (verse 4).

decisions.choice: betrothal: a binding promise of marriage, made before the wedding
decisions.reason: In Jewish and Greek custom a betrothal was a binding agreement, usually arranged by the bride's father, and the bride was expected to stay pure until she was presented to her husband at the wedding. ἡρμοσάμην ("I betrothed") pictures Paul as the one who arranged the match when he brought the gospel to Corinth; he is the church's father in the faith (1 Corinthians 4:15). The presenting looks ahead to Christ's coming (4:14).

decisions.choice: the church as Christ's bride, as Israel was God's bride
decisions.reason: The prophets call Israel the bride of God and call her unfaithfulness adultery (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19-20). Paul applies the picture to the church and Christ, as Ephesians 5:25-27 does. The "pure virgin" is the whole church, and the purity meant is undivided loyalty to Christ, as the next verse says.

decisions.choice: I am like the father who arranged it
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the picture behind "I betrothed you" (m2). Paul may see himself as the father who gives the bride, or more loosely as the one who arranged the marriage.

decisions.choice: a pure virgin bride
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "bride" so that the marriage picture stays clear in one sentence.

records.source: φοβοῦμαι δὲ μή πως, ὡς ὁ ὄφις ἐξηπάτησεν Εὕαν ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ, φθαρῇ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἁπλότητος καὶ τῆς ἁγνότητος τῆς εἰς τὸν Χριστόν.
records.gloss: I fear but lest somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by the cunning of him, may be corrupted the minds of you from the sincerity and the purity the [one] toward the Christ.
pieces: Yet I fear that, in the way the serpent's cunning tricked Eve, your minds may somehow be spoiled and turned away from simple, pure loyalty to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.3: But I fear that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be corrupted [and led away] from the sincerity and the purity that [is] toward {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.3: But I am worried. Long ago the snake was clever and tricked Eve. In the same way, your minds could be led astray, and you could stop being loyal to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} with a pure and undivided heart.

decisions.choice: Genesis 3: the serpent deceiving Eve
decisions.reason: In Genesis 3:1-13 the serpent, the most cunning of the animals, deceives Eve, and she says, "The serpent deceived me" (3:13). Paul continues the picture of verse 2: as Eve was led away from loyalty to God by a clever voice, the church, Christ's promised bride, could be led away by the rivals' persuasive words. In verse 14 he names Satan as the one behind such deception.

decisions.choice: corrupted: spoiled and led away from undivided loyalty
alternatives: simplicity in the sense of naivety
decisions.reason: φθαρῇ means to ruin or corrupt, and it was used of a virgin being seduced, which fits the bridal picture. ἁπλότητος is single-mindedness, a heart that is not divided (the same word as "sincerity" in 1:12 in some manuscripts, and "generosity" in 8:2), and ἁγνότητος is purity. Together they describe a bride's wholehearted faithfulness to Christ.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "and the purity" is included
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts have both "the sincerity and the purity", while many others have only "the sincerity", and a few give the two words in the other order. Copyists may have added "purity" from the bridal picture of verse 2, or dropped it because the two similar words stood side by side. The SBLGNT includes it. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: snake
decisions.reason: "Serpent" is a book word; Readable uses the common word. Literal and Balanced keep "serpent", as Genesis 3 has it.

records.source: εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἄλλον Ἰησοῦν κηρύσσει ὃν οὐκ ἐκηρύξαμεν, ἢ πνεῦμα ἕτερον λαμβάνετε ὃ οὐκ ἐλάβετε, ἢ εὐαγγέλιον ἕτερον ὃ οὐκ ἐδέξασθε, καλῶς ἀνέχεσθε.
records.gloss: If indeed for the [one] coming another Jesus preaches whom not we preached, or a spirit different you receive which not you received, or a gospel different which not you accepted, well you put up with [it].
pieces: When anyone turns up and preaches another Jesus than the one we preached, or you take in a spirit unlike the one you received, or a gospel unlike the one you welcomed, you tolerate it splendidly!

L.4: For if the one who comes preaches another Jesus whom we did not preach, or you receive a different spirit which you did not receive, or a different gospel which you did not accept, you put up with [it] well.

R.4: Someone comes to you and tells you about a different Jesus from the Jesus we told you about. Or you accept a spirit that is not the Spirit you received before. Or you accept good news that is different from the good news you believed. And you put up with it so easily!

decisions.choice: the one who comes: any visiting teacher of this kind, the rivals
alternatives: a single leader among the rivals
decisions.reason: ὁ ἐρχόμενος is singular, but it most likely stands for whoever comes, the visiting teachers Paul calls false apostles in verse 13. The phrase marks them as outsiders who arrived after Paul had founded the church (10:14-15).

decisions.choice: another Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel: a false message about Jesus
decisions.reason: The rivals preach a Jesus with a message Paul does not recognize as the gospel. The Corinthians received the Spirit when they believed Paul's preaching (1:21-22; Galatians 3:2), and a different message brings a spirit that is not God's. Galatians 1:6-9 uses the same words, εὐαγγέλιον ἕτερον, of a message that is no gospel at all. What exactly the rivals taught is not said; in chapters 10-13 they boast of their status and powers and despise weakness.

decisions.choice: you put up with it well: bitter irony
decisions.reason: καλῶς ("well, finely") is ironic, as in Mark 7:9. The Corinthians are patient with the rivals' false message, though not with Paul (verse 1).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "you put up with" (present)
alternatives: "you would put up with" (past tense form)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have the verb in a past tense form, which makes the sentence a supposition ("if someone came ..., you would put up with it"); others have the present tense, which says that it is happening. The SBLGNT has the present. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: you tolerate it splendidly!
alternatives: you put up with it well enough
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the irony of the word "well" (m3).

decisions.choice: a spirit that is not the Spirit you received
decisions.reason: Readable names the Holy Spirit as the Spirit the Corinthians received (m2).

records.source: λογίζομαι γὰρ μηδὲν ὑστερηκέναι τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων·
records.gloss: I consider for in nothing to have fallen short of the super-very apostles;
pieces: I count myself not one bit behind the super-apostles.

L.5: For I reckon [that I] have fallen short in nothing of the super-apostles.

R.5: I do not think those so-called super-apostles are any better than I am.

decisions.choice: the super-apostles: Paul's mocking name for the rivals
alternatives: the leading apostles in Jerusalem, such as Peter, James and John
decisions.reason: ὑπερλίαν is an adverb, "beyond measure, exceedingly", and with ἀποστόλων it makes an ironic title: "the extra-special apostles". Paul uses it again in 12:11. Most likely it means the rivals of verses 4 and 13, who claimed to be apostles of higher standing than Paul, and whom he calls false apostles. Some take it to mean the original apostles in Jerusalem, whom the rivals may have claimed as their backing (compare Galatians 2:6, 9); but Paul would hardly call those men servants of Satan (verses 13-15).

decisions.choice: for: the reason the Corinthians can bear with him
decisions.reason: ὑστερηκέναι is "to have fallen short, to be inferior". The "for" gives the ground for Paul's appeal: he is in no way behind those the Corinthians admire, so they should hear him.

decisions.choice: the super-apostles (L, B); those so-called super-apostles (R)
decisions.reason: "Super-apostles" keeps the mockery of Paul's coined title (m1); a respectful phrase such as "most eminent" would lose it. Readable adds "so-called" to make the irony plain. 12:11 uses the same words.

records.source: εἰ δὲ καὶ ἰδιώτης τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλ’ οὐ τῇ γνώσει, ἀλλ’ ἐν παντὶ φανερώσαντες ἐν πᾶσιν εἰς ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: If but even untrained in the speech, yet not in the knowledge, but in every [way] having made [it] plain in all things to you.
pieces: Even if I am untrained in speaking, I am not so in knowledge. We have shown you that plainly, in every way and in all things.

L.6: But even if [I am] untrained in speech, yet [I am] not in knowledge; indeed, in every [way] we have made [this] plain to you in all things.

R.6: Maybe I am not a skilled speaker, but I do know what I am talking about. We have made that very clear to you in every way.

decisions.choice: untrained in speech: not a professional speaker
decisions.reason: ἰδιώτης is a layman, someone without professional training in a skill. In Greek cities speakers trained in rhetoric were admired and paid, and Paul's critics said his speech was contemptible (10:10). Paul had chosen not to rely on polished speech (1 Corinthians 2:1-5). He grants the point about his speaking but not about his knowledge of the truth.

decisions.choice: we have made it plain: Paul's knowledge has been shown openly to the Corinthians
alternatives: the truth has been made plain
decisions.reason: φανερώσαντες is a participle with no main verb, and the plural is Paul's "we", himself with his companions or himself alone (1:8). What has been made plain is probably his knowledge, shown in everything he did and taught among them. The sentence is compressed, and the words supplied make it complete.

records.source: Ἢ ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησα ἐμαυτὸν ταπεινῶν ἵνα ὑμεῖς ὑψωθῆτε, ὅτι δωρεὰν τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εὐαγγέλιον εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν;
records.gloss: Or a sin did I commit myself humbling so that you might be exalted, because free of charge the of the God gospel I preached to you?
pieces: Or was it a sin on my part to lower myself so that you could be lifted up, by proclaiming God's gospel to you without charging you anything?

L.7: Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?

R.7: I made myself low so that you could be lifted up. I told you God's good news and did not ask you to pay me anything. Was that a sin?

decisions.choice: preaching free of charge: refusing pay from the Corinthians
decisions.reason: Traveling teachers and philosophers were usually paid fees or supported by wealthy patrons. In Corinth Paul worked at his trade instead (Acts 18:3) and refused support from the church, so that no one could say he preached for money (1 Corinthians 9:12-18). Some Corinthians seem to have taken this as an insult, or as a sign that he was no true apostle (12:13).

decisions.choice: humbling myself: lowering his status by manual work
decisions.reason: ταπεινῶν is to make low. Working with his hands put Paul on the level of a laborer, which people of standing despised (1 Corinthians 4:12). The purpose was that the Corinthians would be raised up through the gospel, as Christ became poor to make others rich (8:9).

decisions.choice: a question full of irony
decisions.reason: Paul asks whether his free preaching was a sin because his critics treat it as one. The answer he expects is no.

records.source: ἄλλας ἐκκλησίας ἐσύλησα λαβὼν ὀψώνιον πρὸς τὴν ὑμῶν διακονίαν, καὶ παρὼν πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ ὑστερηθεὶς οὐ κατενάρκησα οὐθενός· τὸ γὰρ ὑστέρημά μου προσανεπλήρωσαν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ ἐλθόντες ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας· καὶ ἐν παντὶ ἀβαρῆ ἐμαυτὸν ὑμῖν ἐτήρησα καὶ τηρήσω.
records.gloss: Other churches I robbed, having received wages for the of you service, \v 9 and being present with you and having been in need, not I burdened anyone; for the need of me supplied the brothers having come from Macedonia; and in everything unburdensome myself to you I kept and I will keep.
pieces: I plundered other churches, accepting pay from them so that I could serve you.

And while I was there with you and ran short, I was a weight on no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia made up what I lacked. In every way I have made sure I cost you nothing, and I will keep it that way.

L.8: I robbed other churches, taking wages [from them] for the service of you,
L.9: and when I was present with you and was in need, I burdened no one; for my need the brothers coming from Macedonia supplied; and in everything I kept myself from being a burden to you, and I will keep [myself so].

R.8: Other churches paid me so that I could serve you. It was almost like robbing them!
R.9: When I was with you and needed something, I did not ask any of you for help. The brothers who came from Macedonia brought me what I needed. I have never let myself be a load on you, and I never will.

decisions.choice: robbed, taking wages: a soldier's words, used with deliberate exaggeration
decisions.reason: ἐσύλησα means to strip or plunder, as soldiers stripped a defeated enemy, and ὀψώνιον is a soldier's ration money, his pay. Paul says, with mock severity, that he took gifts from other churches, which were themselves poor (8:1-2), so that the Corinthians could have the gospel for nothing.

decisions.choice: the brothers from Macedonia: messengers bringing gifts from the churches there
decisions.reason: Macedonia was the Roman province to the north of Achaia, with the churches of Philippi and Thessalonica. The Philippians sent Paul gifts more than once (Philippians 4:15-16), and Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia while he was in Corinth (Acts 18:5). These brothers were most likely particular men who carried the gift.

decisions.choice: burden: to be a dead weight on someone's resources
decisions.reason: κατενάρκησα is a rare word, used in the New Testament only by Paul (12:13-14). It means to weigh someone down, here by living at their expense. ἀβαρῆ, "not burdensome", says the same thing.

decisions.choice: It was almost like robbing them!
decisions.reason: Readable keeps Paul's word but says that it is an exaggeration (m1).

decisions.choice: brothers, without a gender setting
decisions.reason: The brothers who brought the gift were most likely particular men (m2), so no gender setting is used, as in 8:23.

records.source: ἔστιν ἀλήθεια Χριστοῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ ὅτι ἡ καύχησις αὕτη οὐ φραγήσεται εἰς ἐμὲ ἐν τοῖς κλίμασι τῆς Ἀχαΐας.
records.gloss: Is [the] truth of Christ in me that the boasting this not will be stopped as to me in the regions of the Achaia.
pieces: I declare by the truth of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} that is in me: this boast of mine will not be silenced anywhere in the districts of Achaia.

L.10: [As] the truth of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} is in me, this boasting will not be silenced as to me in the regions of Achaia.

R.10: I have the truth of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} in me, so I promise you this: no one anywhere in the province of Achaia will stop me from boasting that I preached to you for free.

decisions.choice: a solemn assurance, close to an oath
decisions.reason: "The truth of Christ is in me" is a way of making a solemn statement, as Romans 9:1 ("I am speaking the truth in Christ") and 2 Corinthians 1:18 and 11:31 are. Paul stakes his truthfulness on his belonging to Christ.

decisions.choice: this boasting: his pride in preaching without pay
decisions.reason: καύχησις refers back to verses 7-9: Paul's boast is that he has preached free of charge, as in 1 Corinthians 9:15, where he says that no one will empty his boast. φραγήσεται is "to be stopped up", as a mouth is shut (Romans 3:19).

decisions.choice: Achaia: the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth its capital
decisions.reason: The letter is addressed to the church in Corinth and to all God's people in Achaia (1:1). Paul will not take support from anyone in the province.

decisions.choice: boast, boasting
decisions.reason: In chapters 10-12 Paul's argument turns on the word itself, so every level keeps "boast" (docs/corinthians-terms.md), where 1:12 has "take pride" at Balanced and Readable.

decisions.choice: that I preached to you for free
decisions.reason: Readable says what the boast is (m2).

records.source: διὰ τί;
records.gloss: Through what?
pieces: Why so?

R.11: Why do I refuse to take your money?

decisions.choice: Why do I refuse to take your money?
decisions.reason: Readable says what the question is about, which the verses before make clear.

records.source: ὅτι οὐκ ἀγαπῶ ὑμᾶς;
records.gloss: Because not I love you?
pieces: Because I do not love you?

L.11: Because I do not love you?

R.11: Is it because I do not love you?

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: Some in Corinth may have taken Paul's refusal of their support as a sign that he did not want close ties with them, since accepting a gift created a bond of friendship. Paul raises the charge in order to deny it.

records.source: ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν.
records.gloss: The God knows.
pieces: God knows I do!

R.11: God knows that I do love you!

decisions.choice: God knows: calling God as witness that he does love them
decisions.reason: Paul calls on God as the witness of what is in his heart, as in verse 31 and 12:2-3. The words answer the question before them: he does love the Corinthians.

decisions.choice: I do; that I do love you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add the answer so that "God knows" is not heard as a shrug (m1).

records.source: Ὃ δὲ ποιῶ καὶ ποιήσω, ἵνα ἐκκόψω τὴν ἀφορμὴν τῶν θελόντων ἀφορμήν, ἵνα ἐν ᾧ καυχῶνται εὑρεθῶσιν καθὼς καὶ ἡμεῖς.
records.gloss: What but I do also I will do, so that I may cut off the opportunity of those wanting an opportunity, so that in what they boast they may be found just as also we.
pieces: And I will go on doing what I am doing, to deny an opening to those who look for one: an opening to boast that they are on the same footing as we are.

L.12: But what I am doing I will also [keep] doing, so that I may cut off the opportunity of those who want an opportunity, so that in what they boast [of] they may be found [to be] just as we [are].

R.12: I will keep on working without pay from you. Those people want a chance to boast that they are just like us. I am not going to give them that chance.

decisions.choice: the rivals want to be seen as Paul's equals in the work they boast of
alternatives: Paul refuses pay so that the rivals, who take pay, will be found to be no better than Paul in the matter they boast of
Paul hopes the rivals will be shamed into working without pay as he does
decisions.reason: The second "so that" is hard. Most likely it describes the opportunity the rivals want: to be regarded as Paul's equals in the apostleship they boast of. As long as Paul takes nothing, there is a plain difference between him and them, since they accept support (verse 20; 1 Corinthians 9:12). Other readings take the clause as Paul's own aim.

decisions.choice: opportunity: a base of operations, a pretext
decisions.reason: ἀφορμὴν was a military word for a base from which to launch an attack, and so an opening or pretext (5:12; Romans 7:8). The rivals want something they can use against Paul or in their own favor.

decisions.choice: working without pay from you
decisions.reason: Readable says what Paul is doing, from verses 7-9.

records.source: οἱ γὰρ τοιοῦτοι ψευδαπόστολοι, ἐργάται δόλιοι, μετασχηματιζόμενοι εἰς ἀποστόλους Χριστοῦ·
records.gloss: The for such [men are] false apostles, workers deceitful, disguising themselves into apostles of Christ;
pieces: People like that are false apostles and dishonest workers, passing themselves off as apostles of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.13: For such [people are] false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.13: Those people are not real apostles. They are workers who lie to people. They only pretend to be apostles of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: false apostles: people who claim to be sent by Christ but are not
decisions.reason: ψευδαπόστολοι appears only here in the New Testament. An apostle is someone sent with a commission, and Paul's apostleship came from Christ himself (1:1; Galatians 1:1). The rivals claim the same and are not what they claim.

decisions.choice: deceitful workers: teachers at work in the church who use deceit
decisions.reason: ἐργάται was used of those who labor in the gospel (Matthew 9:37-38; 1 Timothy 5:18). δόλιοι means using trickery, as in 4:2, where Paul says he does not use cunning. Compare "the evil workers" of Philippians 3:2.

decisions.choice: disguising themselves: changing their outward appearance
decisions.reason: μετασχηματιζόμενοι is to change the outward form of something, and here to take on a false appearance. Paul uses the verb three times in verses 13-15: the rivals, Satan and Satan's servants all disguise themselves.

records.source: καὶ οὐ θαῦμα, αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ Σατανᾶς μετασχηματίζεται εἰς ἄγγελον φωτός·
records.gloss: And no wonder, himself for the Satan disguises himself into an angel of light;
pieces: No surprise there: Satan himself passes himself off as an angel of light.

L.14: And [it is] no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.

R.14: That should not surprise us. Even Satan makes himself look like a shining angel from heaven.

decisions.choice: Satan: the adversary of God and his people
decisions.reason: Σατανᾶς comes from the Hebrew word for adversary or accuser. Paul has already warned that Satan schemes against the church (2:11) and blinds unbelievers (4:4, where he is "the god of this age").

decisions.choice: an angel of light: a messenger who seems to come from God
decisions.reason: Light belongs to God and his presence (4:6; 1 John 1:5), so an angel of light is one who seems to bring a message from God. Some Jewish writings of the time, such as the Life of Adam and Eve, tell of Satan taking on the brightness of an angel to deceive Eve, which ties this verse to verse 3. Paul does not need that story, however, to make his point: deception looks like the truth.

decisions.choice: a shining angel from heaven
decisions.reason: Readable says what "of light" suggests: an angel who seems to come from God (m2).

records.source: οὐ μέγα οὖν εἰ καὶ οἱ διάκονοι αὐτοῦ μετασχηματίζονται ὡς διάκονοι δικαιοσύνης, ὧν τὸ τέλος ἔσται κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: Not great therefore if also the servants of him disguise themselves as servants of righteousness, of whom the end will be according to the works of them.
pieces: So it is no great thing if his servants also pass themselves off as servants of righteousness. Their end will match what they have done.

L.15: [It is] no great [thing], then, if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness; their end will be according to their works.

R.15: So it is not strange that his servants also pretend to be servants who bring righteousness. In the end they will get what their actions deserve.

decisions.choice: servants of righteousness: those who serve God's work of making people right with him
alternatives: people who simply live good lives
decisions.reason: δικαιοσύνης here recalls 3:9, where Paul calls his work "the ministry of righteousness", and 5:21. The rivals present themselves as ministers of God's saving righteousness while they serve Satan. διάκονοι is the word Paul uses for himself as a servant (3:6; 6:4), and he will claim it again in verse 23.

decisions.choice: their end will match their works: God's judgment
decisions.reason: Everyone will receive what is due for what they have done (5:10; Romans 2:6). Paul leaves the rivals' end to God.

decisions.choice: servants who bring righteousness
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of servants they claim to be (m1) and keeps the key word "righteousness".

records.source: Πάλιν λέγω, μή τίς με δόξῃ ἄφρονα εἶναι εἰ δὲ μή γε, κἂν ὡς ἄφρονα δέξασθέ με, ἵνα κἀγὼ μικρόν τι καυχήσωμαι·
records.gloss: Again I say, not anyone me should think a fool to be; if but not indeed, even if as a fool receive me, so that I too a little something may boast;
pieces: Once more I say it: nobody should think I am a fool. Otherwise, welcome me even as a fool, so that I can boast a little too.

L.16: I say again, let no one think me to be a fool; but if [you do], [then] receive me even as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.

R.16: Let me say it again. I do not want anyone to think I am a fool. But if you do think so, then accept me the way you would accept a fool. Then I can boast a little too, as the others do.

decisions.choice: fool: someone without good sense
decisions.reason: ἄφρονα belongs with ἀφροσύνη (verse 1; see the decision there). Paul is not a fool, but the boasting the situation forces on him is the kind of thing a fool does. So he asks to be received as a fool, and he speaks the part. It is not the word for the foolishness of the cross in 1 Corinthians 1-3.

decisions.choice: otherwise: if you do think me a fool
decisions.reason: εἰ δὲ μή γε is a fixed phrase meaning "but if not, otherwise", and κἂν means "at least, even if only": if they insist on taking him for a fool, they should at least give him a fool's hearing.

decisions.choice: I too: as the rivals do
decisions.reason: κἀγὼ ("I too") sets Paul beside the rivals, who boast (verses 12 and 18).

decisions.choice: as the others do
decisions.reason: Readable says who the others are (m3).

records.heading: Paul boasts like a fool

records.source: ὃ λαλῶ οὐ κατὰ κύριον λαλῶ, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ, ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως.
records.gloss: What I speak not according to [the] Lord I speak, but as in foolishness, in this the confidence of the boasting.
pieces: What I say with this confidence in boasting is not said in the Lord's way, but as it were in foolishness.

L.17: What I am speaking, I am not speaking according to [the] Lord, but as in foolishness, in this confidence of boasting.

R.17: When I boast so confidently like this, I am not talking the way the Lord would talk. I am talking like a fool.

decisions.choice: not according to the Lord: not in the way the Lord acts and speaks
alternatives: not inspired by the Lord, not part of Scripture
decisions.reason: κατὰ κύριον means in keeping with the Lord, his humble and gentle ways (10:1) and his rule that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord (10:17). Paul admits that boasting about himself does not match the Lord's way. He is not saying that these words lack the Lord's authority.

decisions.choice: confidence: this bold, self-assured kind of boasting
alternatives: the matter, the subject of boasting
decisions.reason: ὑποστάσει can mean the confidence a person has or the subject in hand. Paul uses the same phrase in 9:4 for a confidence he might be ashamed of. Here it is the bold self-confidence of the boaster whose part he plays.

decisions.choice: like a fool
decisions.reason: Readable keeps "fool" and makes the comparison plain.

records.source: ἐπεὶ πολλοὶ καυχῶνται κατὰ σάρκα, κἀγὼ καυχήσομαι.
records.gloss: Since many boast according to flesh, I too will boast.
pieces: Since many are boasting by merely human standards, I will boast too.

L.18: Since many boast according to [the] flesh, I too will boast.

R.18: Many people boast the way selfish people do, so I will boast too.

decisions.choice: according to the flesh: by merely human standards
decisions.reason: κατὰ σάρκα means judged by what is merely human: family, nation, achievements and outward show, which Paul lists in verses 22-23, as he does in Philippians 3:4-6. The "many" are the rivals. Paul has said that he does not wage war according to the flesh (10:2-3); now, in his fool's speech, he will boast on their terms for a while.

decisions.choice: by merely human standards (B); the way selfish people do (R)
decisions.reason: "Flesh" suggests the body to a modern reader. Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable give the sense (m1), in the same words as 10:2.

records.source: ἡδέως γὰρ ἀνέχεσθε τῶν ἀφρόνων φρόνιμοι ὄντες·
records.gloss: Gladly for you put up with the fools wise being;
pieces: You are wise people, after all, and so you happily bear with fools!

L.19: For you gladly put up with fools, being wise [yourselves].

R.19: You are so wise! That is why you are happy to put up with fools.

decisions.choice: irony: the Corinthians think themselves wise
decisions.reason: Paul does not mean that they are wise. As in 1 Corinthians 4:10 ("you are wise in Christ"), he turns their opinion of themselves against them: people so wise ought not to welcome fools, yet they welcome the rivals, and so they can welcome Paul's foolishness too. φρόνιμοι ("wise, sensible") and ἀφρόνων ("fools, senseless") are a play on words in the Greek.

records.source: ἀνέχεσθε γὰρ εἴ τις ὑμᾶς καταδουλοῖ, εἴ τις κατεσθίει, εἴ τις λαμβάνει, εἴ τις ἐπαίρεται, εἴ τις εἰς πρόσωπον ὑμᾶς δέρει.
records.gloss: You put up with for if someone you enslaves, if someone devours, if someone takes, if someone exalts himself, if someone into [the] face you strikes.
pieces: Indeed you put up with it if someone holds you in bondage, if someone eats you up, if someone takes you in, if someone lords it over you, if someone hits you in the face.

L.20: For you put up with [it] if someone enslaves you, if someone devours [you], if someone takes [you], if someone is lifted up [over you], if someone strikes you in the face.

R.20: You let people make you serve them. You let them take everything you have. You let them trick you. You let them act as if they are better than you. You even let them slap you in the face!

decisions.choice: five kinds of abuse by the rivals: control, exploiting, trapping, arrogance, insult
decisions.reason: καταδουλοῖ is to reduce to slavery, to bring under someone's control (Galatians 2:4). κατεσθίει is to eat up, to exploit people's resources (Mark 12:40). λαμβάνει, here without an object, means to catch or take advantage of, as in 12:16, where Paul is accused of catching the Corinthians by a trick. ἐπαίρεται is to lift oneself up, to act arrogantly (10:5). Everything the rivals do is the opposite of Paul, who would not burden anyone (verse 9).

decisions.choice: struck in the face: a deep insult
alternatives: a figure of speech for humiliating treatment only
decisions.reason: A slap in the face was the classic insult (Matthew 5:39; Acts 23:2). Paul may mean that the rivals actually struck people, or he may use the picture for the contempt with which they treated the church.

decisions.choice: take everything you have; trick you
decisions.reason: Readable says what the pictures mean (m1).

decisions.choice: holds you in bondage (B); make you serve them (R)
decisions.reason: "Enslave" becomes "hold in bondage" in Balanced and "make ... serve" in Readable (style guide); the meaning decision (m1) keeps that the rivals bring them under their control, and Literal keeps "enslaves".

records.source: κατὰ ἀτιμίαν λέγω, ὡς ὅτι ἡμεῖς ἠσθενήκαμεν· ἐν ᾧ δ’ ἄν τις τολμᾷ, ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ λέγω, τολμῶ κἀγώ.
records.gloss: According to shame I say, as that we have been weak; in whatever but anyone dares, in foolishness I speak, dare also I.
pieces: I must say, to our shame, that we have been far too weak to act like that! But whatever anyone else dares to boast of (I am talking in foolishness), I dare to boast of it too.

L.21: I say [it] to [our] shame: we have been weak! But in whatever anyone dares, I am speaking in foolishness, I too dare.

R.21: I am ashamed to admit it, but we were not strong enough to treat you like that! But if others dare to boast about something, then I dare to boast about it too. (I am talking like a fool.)

decisions.choice: mock shame: we were too weak to treat you as the rivals do
alternatives: Paul repeats the charge his critics make, that he is weak
decisions.reason: Paul says with irony that he must confess, to his shame, a weakness: he never abused the Corinthians as the rivals do (verse 20). ὡς ὅτι can mean "as if", reporting how others see it, so the clause may also echo the charge that he is weak (10:10). Either way the irony is the same: what they call weakness is his refusal to exploit them.

decisions.choice: in whatever anyone dares: whatever the rivals are bold enough to claim
decisions.reason: τολμᾷ is to dare, to be bold, Paul's word in 10:2 and 10:12. The claims meant are those he is about to list (verses 22-23), so the boldness is boasting. The words "I am speaking in foolishness" break in as an aside.

decisions.choice: dares to boast of
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the daring is (m2). "Boast" is supplied, so Literal does not have it. "Dare" matches 10:2 and 10:12.

records.source: Ἑβραῖοί εἰσιν;
records.gloss: Hebrews are they?
pieces: Are they Hebrews?

decisions.choice: Hebrews: Jews of Hebrew-speaking heritage
decisions.reason: Ἑβραῖοί was used of Jews who kept the language and customs of their ancestors, often in contrast with Greek-speaking Jews (Acts 6:1). Paul calls himself "a Hebrew born of Hebrews" (Philippians 3:5). The rivals were evidently Jewish believers who boasted of their descent.

records.source: κἀγώ.
records.gloss: I too.
pieces: So am I.

decisions.choice: I too: a short, emphatic answer
decisions.reason: κἀγώ is "I also". The same reply answers each question in this verse, giving the passage its sharp rhythm.

records.source: Ἰσραηλῖταί εἰσιν;
records.gloss: Israelites are they?
pieces: Are they Israelites?

decisions.choice: Israelites: members of God's covenant people
decisions.reason: Ἰσραηλῖταί names the people God chose and to whom the covenants and promises belong (Romans 9:4; 11:1).

records.source: κἀγώ.
records.gloss: I too.
pieces: So am I.

records.source: σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ εἰσιν;
records.gloss: Seed of Abraham are they?
pieces: Are they offspring of Abraham?

decisions.choice: seed of Abraham: heirs of the promises made to Abraham
decisions.reason: σπέρμα ("seed") means descendants. To be Abraham's descendants was to share in the promises God made to him (Romans 11:1; Galatians 3:16, 29). The three titles move from language and heritage to covenant people to the promise.

decisions.choice: offspring (B); descendants (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "seed"; Balanced and Readable use words a modern reader understands as family descent.

records.source: κἀγώ.
records.gloss: I too.
pieces: So am I.

records.source: διάκονοι Χριστοῦ εἰσιν;
records.gloss: Servants of Christ are they?
pieces: Are they servants of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}?

decisions.choice: a claim granted for the sake of argument
decisions.reason: Paul has called the rivals servants of Satan who pose as servants of righteousness (verses 13-15). Here he takes up their claim to be servants of Christ without granting it, to show that by the measure of service he outdoes them. διάκονοι is the word of 3:6 and 6:4.

records.source: παραφρονῶν λαλῶ, ὑπὲρ ἐγώ· ἐν κόποις περισσοτέρως, ἐν φυλακαῖς περισσοτέρως, ἐν πληγαῖς ὑπερβαλλόντως, ἐν θανάτοις πολλάκις·
records.gloss: Being out of my mind I speak, more I; in labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in blows beyond measure, in deaths often;
pieces: I am talking as if I had lost my mind, but I am a better one: with far more labors, far more imprisonments, beatings past counting, and brushes with death again and again.

L.23: I speak as one out of [my] mind: I [am] more; in labors far more, in prisons far more, in beatings beyond measure, in deaths often.

R.23: I am talking like someone who has gone crazy, but I serve {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} even more than they do. I have worked much harder. I have been in prison more often. I have been beaten more times than I can count. Many times I almost died.

decisions.choice: out of my mind: beyond foolishness, like a madman
decisions.reason: παραφρονῶν is stronger than the foolishness of verses 1, 16-17 and 21: it means to be beside oneself, insane. To compare himself with the rivals as their better is, Paul says, madness.

decisions.choice: I more: I am a servant of Christ even more than they
decisions.reason: ὑπὲρ ἐγώ ("more, I") is compressed. Paul does not deny the title but claims more right to it, and the proof is not success but suffering.

decisions.choice: deaths: times of mortal danger
decisions.reason: θανάτοις, plural, means situations in which he nearly died (1:9-10; 4:11).

decisions.choice: imprisonments and beatings: only some are recorded in Acts
decisions.reason: Before this letter Acts records one imprisonment, at Philippi, with a beating (Acts 16:22-24); Paul refers to others the record does not include. The list is the fullest account of his sufferings in the New Testament (compare 6:4-5; 1 Corinthians 4:9-13).

decisions.choice: with far more labors, far more imprisonments, beatings past counting
alternatives: I have worked much harder, been in prison more
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the list form of the Greek, a string of phrases without verbs, so that its rhythm can be heard.

decisions.choice: I serve Christ even more than they do
decisions.reason: Readable completes Paul's compressed claim (m2).

records.source: ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων πεντάκις τεσσεράκοντα παρὰ μίαν ἔλαβον, τρὶς ἐραβδίσθην, ἅπαξ ἐλιθάσθην, τρὶς ἐναυάγησα, νυχθήμερον ἐν τῷ βυθῷ πεποίηκα·
records.gloss: By Jews five times forty less one I received, \v 25 three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked, a night and a day in the deep I have spent;
pieces: Five times the Jewish authorities gave me the forty lashes less one.
Three times I was flogged with rods; once I was stoned; three times my ship was wrecked; a night and a day I have spent out on the deep.

L.24: From [the] Jews five times I received forty [lashes] less one;
L.25: three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked, a night and a day I have spent in the deep.

R.24: Five times the Jewish leaders had me whipped thirty-nine times.
R.25: Three times I was beaten with rods. Once people threw stones at me to kill me. Three times I was on a ship that was wrecked. Once I spent a whole night and day floating in the sea.

decisions.choice: forty lashes less one: the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine strokes
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 25:3 limits a flogging to forty strokes. Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so as not to break the law by miscounting, as the later rules of the Mishnah also show. The punishment was given by synagogue authorities to Jews, so Paul kept going to the synagogues as a member of his people and accepted their discipline. Acts records none of these five floggings.

decisions.choice: beaten with rods: a Roman punishment carried out by city officials
decisions.reason: ἐραβδίσθην is the punishment given by the attendants of Roman magistrates, who carried rods. At Philippi Paul and Silas were beaten this way, though Paul was a Roman citizen (Acts 16:22-23, 37). The other two occasions are not recorded.

decisions.choice: stoned once: at Lystra
decisions.reason: At Lystra a crowd stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, thinking he was dead (Acts 14:19).

decisions.choice: shipwrecked three times, a full day and night adrift
decisions.reason: None of these shipwrecks is in Acts; the wreck on the way to Rome (Acts 27) came later. νυχθήμερον is a night and a day, a full twenty-four hours, and βυθῷ is the deep, the open sea. The perfect πεποίηκα ("I have spent") makes the memory vivid.

decisions.choice: the Jewish authorities (B); the Jewish leaders (R)
decisions.reason: The punishment was given by synagogue authorities (m1); Balanced and Readable say so, so that "the Jews" is not heard as the whole people.

decisions.choice: thirty-nine times
decisions.reason: Readable gives the number plainly (m1). Literal and Balanced keep the Greek way of counting, which recalls the limit of forty in Deuteronomy.

records.source: ὁδοιπορίαις πολλάκις, κινδύνοις ποταμῶν, κινδύνοις λῃστῶν, κινδύνοις ἐκ γένους, κινδύνοις ἐξ ἐθνῶν, κινδύνοις ἐν πόλει, κινδύνοις ἐν ἐρημίᾳ, κινδύνοις ἐν θαλάσσῃ, κινδύνοις ἐν ψευδαδέλφοις, κόπῳ καὶ μόχθῳ, ἐν ἀγρυπνίαις πολλάκις, ἐν λιμῷ καὶ δίψει, ἐν νηστείαις πολλάκις, ἐν ψύχει καὶ γυμνότητι·
records.gloss: In journeys often, in dangers of rivers, in dangers of robbers, in dangers from race, in dangers from Gentiles, in dangers in city, in dangers in wilderness, in dangers in sea, in dangers among false brothers, \v 27 in labor and toil, in sleeplessnesses often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness;
pieces: Again and again I have been on the road, facing dangers from rivers, dangers from bandits, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the open country, dangers at sea, dangers among false {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}};
in labor and weariness, many nights without sleep, in hunger and thirst, many days going without food, in cold and with too little to wear.

L.26: [On] journeys often, [in] dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from [my own] people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in [the] city, dangers in [the] wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}};
L.27: in labor and toil, in sleepless nights often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness.

R.26: I have traveled from place to place many times. Rivers have put me in danger, and so have robbers. I have been in danger from my own Jewish people and from people who are not Jews. I have been in danger in cities, in the wild country, and at sea. I have been in danger from false {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, people who pretended to belong to God's family.
R.27: I have worked hard and been worn out. Many nights I could not sleep. I have been hungry and thirsty. Often I have had nothing to eat. I have been cold and did not have enough clothes to keep warm.

decisions.choice: the dangers of travel by road and sea
decisions.reason: Paul traveled thousands of miles, mostly on foot. Rivers had few bridges and could flood without warning, and bandits were a known danger on roads through mountains and lonely country. ἐρημίᾳ is uninhabited country, not necessarily desert.

decisions.choice: from my own people, from Gentiles: opposition from Jews and from non-Jews
decisions.reason: γένους ("race") means Paul's own people, the Jews; Acts tells of plots and attacks by Jewish opponents (Acts 9:23, 29; 13:50; 14:19; 17:5) and of trouble stirred up by Gentiles (Acts 16:19-22; 19:23-41).

decisions.choice: false brothers: people who claimed to be fellow believers but were not
decisions.reason: ψευδαδέλφοις is used in Galatians 2:4 of people who slipped into the church to spy on its freedom. It is masculine plural, the ordinary way to speak of a group that may include women as well as men.

decisions.choice: fastings: going without food, perhaps sometimes by choice
alternatives: going without food only because there was none
decisions.reason: νηστείαις usually means fasting. Here it stands next to "hunger and thirst", which suggests something different from simple want, perhaps food given up for the sake of the work; but in this list of hardships it may mean going hungry for lack of time or means, as in 6:5.

decisions.choice: labor and toil, cold and nakedness: hard work, and too little clothing
decisions.reason: κόπῳ and μόχθῳ are a common pair for exhausting work (1 Thessalonians 2:9), as Paul supported himself by his trade. γυμνότητι is not literal nakedness but having too little to wear against the cold (1 Corinthians 4:11).

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: False believers of both sexes are meant (m3), so the default is inclusive, with "brothers" as the traditional form.

decisions.choice: dangers ... dangers
alternatives: a single "in danger from" followed by a list
decisions.reason: The Greek repeats its word for danger eight times. Balanced repeats "dangers" each time to keep the rhythm of the list.

decisions.choice: people who pretended to belong to God's family
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word (m3).

records.source: χωρὶς τῶν παρεκτὸς ἡ ἐπίστασίς μοι ἡ καθ’ ἡμέραν, ἡ μέριμνα πασῶν τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν.
records.gloss: Apart from the things besides, the pressure on me the daily, the concern of all the churches.
pieces: And apart from all these other things, there is what presses on me day after day: my anxious care for all the churches.

L.28: Apart from the things besides [these], [there is] the daily pressure on me, the concern for all the churches.

R.28: And that is not all. Every day I feel the weight of caring for all the churches.

decisions.choice: apart from the other things: besides everything not mentioned
decisions.reason: παρεκτὸς can mean "besides, apart from" or "outside". Paul may mean the many other things he has not listed, or the outward troubles just named, set against the inner burden that follows.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "pressure"
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts have the word for pressure or a crowding in on someone; many later manuscripts have a longer word meaning an attack or rush of people upon him. The sense differs little. The SBLGNT has the first. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: concern for all the churches: an anxious care for them
decisions.reason: μέριμνα is anxiety or concern. Paul tells the Philippians not to be anxious about anything (Philippians 4:6), but here it is the proper care of one who is responsible for others (1 Corinthians 12:25).

records.source: τίς ἀσθενεῖ, καὶ οὐκ ἀσθενῶ;
records.gloss: Who is weak, and not I am weak?
pieces: Is anyone weak without my feeling weak as well?

L.29: Who is weak, and I am not weak?

R.29: When someone is weak, I feel weak too.

decisions.choice: weak: any weakness, including weakness of faith or conscience
decisions.reason: ἀσθενεῖ is the word for the weak believers of 1 Corinthians 8:7-13 and 9:22, where Paul became weak to win the weak. Here he shares in the weakness of others. The theme of weakness leads into verse 30.

records.source: τίς σκανδαλίζεται καὶ οὐκ ἐγὼ πυροῦμαι;
records.gloss: Who is caused to fall, and not I burn?
pieces: Is anyone made to fall without my burning inside?

L.29: Who is caused to fall, and I do not burn?

R.29: When someone is made to fall into sin, I burn inside.

decisions.choice: caused to fall: led into sin
decisions.reason: σκανδαλίζεται is the verb of 1 Corinthians 8:13: to be made to stumble and fall, to be led into sin or away from faith.

decisions.choice: I burn: with distress and indignation
decisions.reason: πυροῦμαι is to be set on fire, here inwardly. It can be indignation against whoever caused the fall, or the pain of sharing the fallen person's distress, or both. The verb is the same as in 1 Corinthians 7:9, where it means burning with desire, which does not fit here.

records.source: Εἰ καυχᾶσθαι δεῖ, τὰ τῆς ἀσθενείας μου καυχήσομαι.
records.gloss: If to boast it is necessary, the things of the weakness of me I will boast.
pieces: If boast I must, my boasting will be about the things that belong to my weakness.

L.30: If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of the things of my weakness.

R.30: If I have to boast, I will boast about the ways I am weak.

decisions.choice: boasting of weakness: the turn in Paul's argument
decisions.reason: Paul now says plainly what his list has been doing: he boasts not of strength but of what shows him weak, because in weakness Christ's power is seen (12:5, 9-10). This fits the rule he has taken from Jeremiah 9:23-24: whoever boasts should boast in the Lord (10:17; 1 Corinthians 1:31).

decisions.choice: if I must: boasting forced on him
decisions.reason: δεῖ expresses necessity. The rivals' claims and the Corinthians' doubts force Paul to boast (12:1, 11).

records.source: ὁ θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ οἶδεν, ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, ὅτι οὐ ψεύδομαι.
records.gloss: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus knows, the [one] being blessed into the ages, that not I am lying.
pieces: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, the one who is blessed for all ages, knows that what I say is no lie.

L.31: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus knows, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} who is blessed to the ages, that I am not lying.

R.31: God, the Father of the Lord Jesus, knows that I am not lying. God deserves praise forever!

decisions.choice: an oath: God is witness that Paul tells the truth
decisions.reason: Paul calls God as witness to the truth of what he says, as in 1:23, Galatians 1:20 and Romans 9:1. The oath may cover the whole list, or it may introduce the story of Damascus that follows, which might seem hard to believe or might be told against him.

decisions.choice: the one who is blessed forever: God the Father
decisions.reason: ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς most naturally refers to God, the subject of the sentence, as in Romans 1:25 and 2 Corinthians 1:3. It is praise: God is the one who is worthy of blessing for all ages.

decisions.choice: God deserves praise forever!
decisions.reason: Readable moves the praise into its own sentence so that the oath stays clear.

records.source: ἐν Δαμασκῷ ὁ ἐθνάρχης Ἁρέτα τοῦ βασιλέως ἐφρούρει τὴν πόλιν Δαμασκηνῶν πιάσαι με, καὶ διὰ θυρίδος ἐν σαργάνῃ ἐχαλάσθην διὰ τοῦ τείχους καὶ ἐξέφυγον τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: In Damascus the ethnarch of Aretas the king was guarding the city of [the] Damascenes to seize me, \v 33 and through a window in a basket I was let down through the wall and escaped the hands of him.
pieces: In Damascus, the ruler appointed by King Aretas set a watch on the city of the Damascenes to catch me.
But I was let down through an opening in the wall in a rope basket, and I escaped from his grasp.

L.32: In Damascus the ethnarch of Aretas the king was guarding the city of [the] Damascenes to seize me,
L.33: and through a window I was let down in a basket through the wall, and I escaped his hands.

R.32: When I was in the city of Damascus, the governor who served King Aretas had guards watching the city so that they could arrest me.
R.33: But friends put me in a big basket and let me down through a window in the city wall. So I got away from him.

decisions.choice: Aretas and his ethnarch: the Nabatean king and his official
decisions.reason: Aretas IV was king of the Nabateans, the Arab kingdom east and south of Judea with its capital at Petra, from about 9 BC to AD 40. ἐθνάρχης is a ruler or official over a people or district. Whether he controlled Damascus itself or led the Nabatean community there or watched the city from outside is not known.

decisions.choice: the same escape told in Acts 9:23-25
decisions.reason: Acts 9:23-25 says that Jews in Damascus plotted to kill Paul and watched the gates day and night, and that his disciples let him down through the wall in a basket at night. The two accounts tell the same event from different sides: Paul mentions the king's official, Acts the Jewish plotters; both may have worked together.

decisions.choice: window, basket: an opening in the wall, a large woven or rope basket
decisions.reason: θυρίδος is a small window or opening, perhaps in a house built into the city wall, as Rahab's was (Joshua 2:15). σαργάνῃ is a large basket of woven rope or wicker, big enough to hold a man.

decisions.choice: a humiliating escape, told as a boast of weakness
alternatives: a simple record of danger with no further point
decisions.reason: Paul ends his list of boasts with a moment of helplessness: the apostle lowered in a basket and slipping away in the dark. It illustrates verse 30, boasting of weakness. Readers who knew that the Romans gave a crown to the first soldier up an enemy wall may have heard the irony of an apostle who went down one; whether Paul intended that is not certain.

decisions.choice: friends put me in a big basket
alternatives: I was let down in a basket
decisions.reason: Readable names who lowered Paul, from Acts 9:25, which calls them his disciples (m2).

decisions.choice: the ruler appointed by King Aretas
decisions.reason: "Ethnarch" is not common modern English; Balanced describes the office (m1). Literal keeps the Greek title.
